headline: High: TREK’s browser/MCP and secret-handling create default data-leak and cascading-error risks when paired with Plane’s broad network/file-ingest workflow.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: TREK can use MCP and browsers, so it may ingest external or shared content; Plane accepts file uploads and handles hyperlinks/notes, creating a plausible bridge for instruction-like content. No shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than proven. The interaction is pairwise because TREK can surface content that Plane may treat as trusted input.
conditions: IF TREK forwards browser or MCP content into Plane file uploads or notes, injection risk materializes.
IF Plane parses uploaded content as instructions without provenance checks, attacker-controlled text can steer actions.
mitigations: Disable automatic import of browser/MCP content into Plane.
Require manual review before Plane ingests any TREK-generated text.
Tag imported content with source provenance.
Restrict TREK MCP tools to read-only sources.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: TREK touches API keys, MFA secrets, reservations, and email addresses, while Plane handles files, images, hyperlinks, and broad network egress. If the pair shares a workspace or passes artifacts between them, sensitive TREK data can be exposed through Plane’s outbound connectivity. The profiles do not show isolation, so uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF TREK artifacts containing secrets are copied into Plane uploads or notes, leakage occurs.
IF Plane forwards imported files or hyperlinks to external services, sensitive data can leave the environment.
mitigations: Keep TREK secrets out of Plane workspaces.
Block Plane access to secret-bearing files.
Use separate accounts and storage roots.
Review outbound destinations for Plane before enabling imports.
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction on shared artifacts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Plane has broad network egress and file uploads, while TREK is real-time collaborative with multiple instances and MCP/WebSocket-style interaction. They do not both show unrestricted filesystem write, so the strongest conflict indicators are absent. Still, overlapping mutable collaboration surfaces can race if they share resources or OAuth-backed state.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same shared resource through APIs or mounted storage, conflicts can occur.
IF TREK sessions and Plane imports target the same mutable record set, last-write-wins races are possible.
mitigations: Separate writable resources per agent.
Disable concurrent edits on shared records.
Add explicit locking around shared API objects.
Schedule imports outside active collaboration windows.
requires-engineering: implement optimistic concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: TREK is a collaborative planner with AI built in, and Plane can ingest files, notes, and hyperlinks. That makes it plausible that Plane treats TREK output as authoritative and propagates errors into tasks or roadmaps. The pathway is inferred, not directly documented, so medium is appropriate rather than low.
conditions: IF Plane imports TREK-generated itineraries or summaries without verification, errors cascade.
IF TREK AI output is copied into Plane tasks as ground truth, downstream actions may be wrong.
mitigations: Require human verification before copying outputs.
Mark TREK-generated content as untrusted.
Use checklists for imported plans.
Limit Plane automation on imported items.
requires-engineering: add validation against source reservations or maps.

E_compliance.rationale: TREK explicitly handles API keys, MFA secrets, and reservations, while Plane touches files, notes, and issues and offers broad network egress. If regulated or sensitive travel data is moved from TREK into Plane, retention and residency controls may diverge. Only TREK is cited for secret classes because the compliance concern is primarily about its sensitive data flowing into Plane.
conditions: IF EU personal travel data from TREK is stored in Plane without a DPA or residency controls, compliance risk increases.
IF Plane retains imported reservations or identity data longer than TREK, retention mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Avoid moving regulated data into Plane.
Review retention settings in both systems.
Separate EU and non-EU datasets.
Document lawful basis before import.
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing and deletion workflows.
